nodes.label: Authoring toolchain
nodes.summary: What Claude runs to write an explainer: SKILL.md says what to do (write patches, never UI), bin/xpl launches the CLI, and the CLI checks the patches against the static index and rejects what it cannot resolve.

nodes.label: skill
nodes.summary: The Claude skill: SKILL.md (operations, workflow, hard rules), reference/ (every command, the patch format, worked example patches) and bin/xpl, a symlink-safe launcher for the built CLI.

nodes.label: cli
nodes.summary: The `xpl` command: `dispatch` finds the command by name in COMMANDS (index, outline, show, refs, search, new, apply, validate, anchors, resolve, status, view, bundle) and awaits its `run(ctx, args)`.

nodes.label: indexer
nodes.summary: Builds `.explainer/index-<commit>.json` from a repository: file discovery, tree-sitter (WASM) language packs, a heuristic reference resolver, and a SCIP importer whose references replace the heuristic ones, file by file, when the tool ran.

nodes.label: core
nodes.summary: Schema types plus the pure logic on top of them: text hashing, anchors, graph derivation, validation and patch application. Its package.json calls it browser-safe, with no `node:*` imports.

nodes.label: viewer
nodes.summary: The viewer: a React, CodeMirror 6 and elkjs app that Vite builds into one self-contained `dist/index.html`; `main.tsx` loads the bundle from the page and renders the app from it.

nodes.label: Discovery and commit id
nodes.summary: Decides what gets indexed and what the index is called: `discoverFiles` lists and filters the files, `resolveCommitId` picks the id that goes into `index-<commit>.json`.

nodes.label: Parsing and language packs
nodes.summary: Turns one file into facts: `parseFile` builds the tree-sitter tree, and the file's language pack reads symbols, reference sites, imports and type facts from it.

nodes.label: Symbol assembly
nodes.summary: Gives a pack's symbol drafts their identity: `assembleSymbols` builds ids, `~N` suffixes, whole-line ranges and parents, and `FileHasher` hashes the lines.

nodes.label: SCIP precise resolvers
nodes.summary: Supplies the references SCIP indexers report: a registry of resolvers, one per indexer, that run the tool, map its index onto the symbols and report which files they described, so that `buildIndex` can replace the heuristic references of those files.

nodes.label: build-index.ts
nodes.summary: The `xpl index` command: it reads `--precise` (auto, off or require) and `--commit`, calls `buildIndex`, stores the result with `writeIndex` and prints a per-language summary whose `refs:` column comes from `describeRefs`.

nodes.label: build.ts
nodes.summary: `buildIndex` runs the whole pipeline (discover files; per file read, hash, parse, extract, assemble; heuristic references; per-file precise replacement; commit id) and returns the `SymbolIndex` with its warnings; `writeIndex` stores it as `.explainer/index-<commit>.json`.

nodes.label: files.ts
nodes.summary: File discovery: `git ls-files` (tracked plus untracked, minus ignored) inside a git work tree, otherwise a directory walk; binaries, files over 1 MiB, lockfiles and `.explainer/`, `node_modules` and `.git` paths are dropped, and each file gets its language from its extension.

nodes.label: commit.ts
nodes.summary: Names the index: an explicit `--commit`, else the short HEAD of a clean git top level, else `wt-` plus a content hash of the indexed files.

nodes.label: parse.ts
nodes.summary: `ParserPool` keeps one web-tree-sitter parser per grammar and reuses it across files, and `parseFile` returns a `FileContext` (file, language, source, lines and syntax tree) together with the pack that will read it; the tree must be freed with `dispose()`.

nodes.label: types.ts
nodes.summary: The `LanguagePack` contract (`extract`, `classifySite`, `resolveModule`) and the plain facts a pack returns; by contract a pack does not assign ids, `~N` suffixes or hashes and does not resolve references.

nodes.label: typescript.ts
nodes.summary: The TypeScript, TSX and JavaScript pack: `Extractor` walks the syntax tree for symbols and imports and then scans it for call, type, heritage, write and read sites; the pack also holds `resolveModule` and `classifySite`.

nodes.label: hash.ts
nodes.summary: `FileHasher` hashes line ranges of one file the way core's `hashText` does (trim every line, drop blank ones, SHA-256, first 12 hex characters), trimming each line once.

nodes.label: symbols.ts
nodes.summary: `assembleSymbols` turns a pack's symbol drafts into `IndexedSymbol`s (ids, `~N` suffixes, whole-line ranges, hashes, parents), and `SymbolLookup` finds the innermost symbol at a position, which gives reference sites their `from`.

nodes.label: heuristic.ts
nodes.summary: The language-agnostic heuristic resolver: it turns the packs' reference sites into `resolution: "heuristic"` references by following scopes, import bindings and declared types, and drops the sites it cannot resolve.

nodes.label: precise.ts
nodes.summary: The precise-resolver contract and registry: `PreciseResolver.resolve(input)` returns references, a tool name and the files the tool described; `registerPreciseResolver` and `preciseResolvers()` keep the registered resolvers.

nodes.label: resolvers.ts
nodes.summary: One resolver per SCIP indexer (`scipTypescriptResolver`, `scipPythonResolver`, `scipGoResolver`): run the tool, map its index with `mapScip` and return the references, the tool name and the described files.

nodes.label: run.ts
nodes.summary: Runs the pinned SCIP indexers (`npx` for scip-typescript and scip-python, `go run` of scip-go once per go.mod) with a timeout in a temporary directory and decodes the `.scip` files they write.

nodes.label: map.ts
nodes.summary: `mapScip` turns decoded SCIP indexes into references: each non-definition occurrence of a symbol defined in an indexed file gets `from` (the innermost symbol at the occurrence) and `to` (the symbol that is its definition) and is classified by the pack's `classifySite`; the files the index described are reported too.

nodes.label: typescriptPack
nodes.summary: The TypeScript pack serves `typescript`, `tsx` and `javascript` files (JavaScript is parsed with the tsx grammar), derives references heuristically and treats top-level names as visible per file (`packageScope: "file"`).

nodes.label: CLI side of apply
nodes.summary: `xpl apply` on the command line: loads the explainer and the patch, opens the workspace, calls core's `applyPatch`, then writes the result atomically or prints the outcome.

nodes.label: Patch merge and validation
nodes.summary: Core: `applyPatch` merges a patch into a deep clone of the explainer and `validateExplainer` re-checks the result strictly; any surviving error hands back the caller's explainer untouched.

nodes.label: Anchor building and hashing
nodes.summary: Core: `makeAnchor` turns an AnchorInput into a stored anchor (symbol lookup with did-you-mean, `find` or `span` to a line range, hash of the trimmed non-blank lines); `resolveWith` recomputes that hash later.

nodes.label: cli.ts
nodes.summary: CLI entry: `dispatch` looks a command up by name in the `COMMANDS` array and calls its `run(ctx, args)`; `run()` turns a thrown `CliError` into `error: ...` on stderr (or a JSON object with `--json`) and returns its exit code.

nodes.label: commands/apply.ts
nodes.summary: The `apply` command: loads the explainer and the patch, calls `applyPatch`, writes the merged explainer with `atomicWrite` when it was accepted and changed something, and prints the outcome: the changed ids, or a rejection or a refusal for user-protected content with exit code 1.

nodes.label: repo.ts
nodes.summary: Explainer and workspace loading for the commands: `loadExplainer` finds and parses an explainer file, `openWorkspace` picks an index file (`--index`, else the one the explainer is bound to), returns its model plus a cache of working-tree text and warns when the index no longer matches the tree.

nodes.label: fsutil.ts
nodes.summary: File helpers: `atomicWrite` writes a temp file next to the target and renames it into place, `parseJson` turns a JSON syntax error into a `CliError` that names the source and, when it can, the position, `workingTreeReader` reads repo files for the text cache.

nodes.label: format.ts
nodes.summary: Text formatting for command output: `renderIssue` prints one issue as `severity path [element id]: message`, `issueSummary` counts errors and warnings.

nodes.label: core/apply.ts
nodes.summary: `applyPatch` and the `Applier` class: check each patch object against a field spec, upsert nodes, edges, concepts, views and tours into a deep clone of the explainer (shallow merge; for the llm actor, what the user owns is skipped), build the anchors with `makeAnchor`, then validate; on any error the caller's explainer comes back untouched.

nodes.label: validate.ts
nodes.summary: `validateExplainer` and the `Validator` class check a whole explainer against the index and the current text: ids, references, provenance, the status of every anchor and the anchor an llm edge needs inside both of its ends. Each anchor is re-classified with `resolveWith`: drifted and missing ones are errors in strict mode and warnings in lenient mode, and the message says when the user owns the element, so an llm patch cannot repair it.

nodes.label: anchors.ts
nodes.summary: `makeAnchor` builds a stored anchor from an AnchorInput (find or span to a line range, hash of the trimmed non-blank lines, resolved range); `resolveAnchor` and `resolveWith` re-check one stored anchor against the current text as ok, moved, drifted or missing, and `reresolveExplainer` does that for every anchor of an explainer; `TextCache` memoises the text of a file and its lines.

nodes.label: text.ts
nodes.summary: Text and hash helpers: `normalizeLines` trims every line and drops blank ones, `hashText` and `hashNormalized` keep `sha256:` plus the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of that, and `normalizedPrefixHashes` hashes the prefixes of a line sequence from a start line with one running digest. `makeAnchor` and `hashOf` (which `resolveWith` uses) hash the lines of a span anchor with `normalizeLines` and `hashNormalized`, and `searchSpan` uses `normalizedPrefixHashes` to re-find moved code.

nodes.label: index-model.ts
nodes.summary: `IndexModel`: lookups over the symbol index (files, symbols, references); `file` and `symbolAt` resolve an anchor's target, and `suggestFiles` / `suggestSymbols` rank the did-you-mean candidates for a name that is not there.

nodes.label: applyCommand.run
nodes.summary: The `xpl apply` command: it loads the explainer, reads the patch, opens the workspace and runs `applyPatch` as actor `llm` (or `user` with `--actor user`). It writes the merged explainer with `atomicWrite` when the result is ok, not a `--dry-run` and something changed, prints the outcome (or one JSON object with `--json`) and returns 1 when the patch is rejected or when everything it would change is user-protected.

nodes.label: Applier
nodes.summary: One instance per `applyPatch` call: `run` merges the patch into a deep clone `work` of the caller's explainer (`input`), builds the anchors with `makeAnchor`, validates the result strictly and collects the `issues` and `changed` ids; `fail()` returns `input` when an error is left. For the `llm` actor it skips existing elements, views and tours with origin `user`, keeps the fields in `userFields` and refuses to remove what the user owns; for the `user` actor it adds the fields it changes on an element of another origin to `userFields`.

nodes.label: Page data to store
nodes.summary: main.tsx has data.ts read the bundle embedded in the page, core's parseBundle checks its schema, and main.tsx then creates the ViewerStore and renders the app.

nodes.label: State and derivation
nodes.summary: The store holds the selection, the caret and the mode; derive.ts turns a state into what the screen shows (graph, code focus, editor panes, caret matches) and hooks.ts hands the store and that result to React components.

nodes.label: Diagram
nodes.summary: DiagramPane picks the renderer for the current view: a graph (laid out by ELK through graphLayout.ts) or a sequence diagram; the view's own boxes, edges, steps and lifelines carry their element id and select it in the store when clicked.

nodes.label: Code editors
nodes.summary: EditorStack shows one read-only CodeMirror editor per pane (the files of the code focus, plus a file opened by hand) and pushes the highlight and dim decorations into them; editor.ts builds the editors and reports caret and selection changes as a range of lines.

nodes.label: Core linking
nodes.summary: The core functions both directions rest on: graph.ts derives the boxes, edges and stubs of a graph view, stubs.ts decides which ghosts to draw, and focus.ts maps an element to its code and a line of code back to elements.

nodes.label: main.tsx
nodes.summary: Page entry: loadBundle reads the data from the page; when it is there, main.tsx creates the ViewerStore, installs the test hooks and the URL watcher and renders App, otherwise it renders a page with the error message and how to open an explainer.

nodes.label: store.ts
nodes.summary: The viewer's state (view, selection, caret, opened file, mode, tour position, loaded files) and the actions that change it; each change goes through set, which calls the subscribers. Edits of views and tours are also sent to the local server when there is one.

nodes.label: derive.ts
nodes.summary: Turns a ViewerState into what the screen shows, memoised: the derived graph of the current view, the code focus of the selection with the editor panes it needs, and the elements that match the caret.

nodes.label: hooks.ts
nodes.summary: React bindings for the store: useStore returns it, useViewerState subscribes to it with useSyncExternalStore, and useDerived returns getDerived of the current state.

nodes.label: DiagramPane.tsx
nodes.summary: The diagram of the current view under a caption with its title and question: it reads the derived state and renders a GraphView for a graph view or a SequenceView for a sequence view; outside Present the caption of a graph view also carries the stub and edge-kind controls.

nodes.label: GraphView.tsx
nodes.summary: Draws a derived graph as SVG once ELK has laid it out: boxes, edges, stubs and ghost boxes are groups with a data-element-id, a click on a box or an edge selects it in the store, and selected, matched and related elements get the classes is-selected, is-match and is-related.

nodes.label: SequenceView.tsx
nodes.summary: Draws a sequence view as SVG from layoutSequence: frames, lifelines and one row per step; a click on a lifeline or a step selects it, and the same three state classes mark selected, matched and related elements.

nodes.label: graphLayout.ts
nodes.summary: Turns a DerivedGraph into positioned boxes and routed edges with ELK (layered, orthogonal edges, containers as compound nodes); layoutGraphFitting picks the direction that suits the pane, and a grid layout takes over when ELK throws.

nodes.label: EditorStack.tsx
nodes.summary: The code side: one EditorPane per pane that derive.ts lists, each a read-only CodeMirror editor under a file header; the panes receive the focus decorations and the scroll position from the derived state and the caret from the store, and report caret moves back to store.setCursor.

nodes.label: editor.ts
nodes.summary: CodeMirror setup: read-only editors coloured from the page theme, the highlight and dim line decorations of a code focus, and the caret or selection reported as a range of lines.

nodes.label: focus.ts
nodes.summary: Code focus and its reverse: codeFocus lists the ranges an element points at (its anchors, else its structure), mergeFocusByFile merges them per file for the editor, and buildReverseIndex answers which elements cover a line, innermost first.

nodes.label: graph.ts
nodes.summary: Derives what a graph view shows from its include list, the index and the stored edges (nodes with their containers, derived and stored edges, stubs and ghosts), plus the pure view edits the viewer applies: expandStub, drillIn and collapse.

nodes.label: stubs.ts
nodes.summary: The stub policy: a reference with one end outside the view becomes a stub to a ghost box; in the default `top` mode planStubs folds the outside symbols of a partly shown file into one "rest of <file>" ghost, keeps the `max` (default 8) most referenced ghosts and merges the others into "+N more" ghosts, one per direction.

nodes.label: loadBundle
nodes.summary: Finds the `<script id="xpl-data">` element and parses its text with parseBundle; a missing element, a wrong schema or a bundle without explainer or index comes back as `{ ok: false, error }`, anything else as `{ ok: true, bundle }`.

nodes.label: parseBundle
nodes.summary: JSON-parses the text of the bundle script and throws unless its `schema` is `code-explainer/bundle@0`.

nodes.label: ViewerStore
nodes.summary: The state container of the viewer: it keeps a ViewerState, changes it through actions such as click, setCursor and present, and calls its subscribers after each change.

nodes.label: DiagramPane
nodes.summary: Reads the derived state and renders the current view as a GraphView or a SequenceView under a caption; both receive the selection, the caret matches and the related ids, and a graph view also gets the derived graph.

nodes.label: deriveGraph
nodes.summary: Computes what a graph view shows: each reference of a shown kind is lifted to the boxes that stand for its two ends, two different boxes give a derived edge and one end without a box gives a stub; stored edges are laid over them, `hidden` is applied and planStubs picks the ghosts.

nodes.label: GraphView
nodes.summary: Asks layoutGraphFitting to lay the derived graph out for the size of its pane, then draws the result in a pan/zoom canvas; while the layout is pending, when it failed or when the view is empty it shows a message instead.

nodes.label: SequenceView
nodes.summary: Lays the sequence view out with layoutSequence (a memo over the view and the model) and draws its frames, lifelines and step rows in a pan/zoom canvas.

nodes.label: EditorPane
nodes.summary: The editor of one file: it creates the CodeMirror view once the text is there, then pushes the pane's focus decorations, the scroll position and the store's caret into it, and passes editor.ts a callback that forwards caret moves to store.setCursor.

nodes.label: resolveCommand.run
nodes.summary: The `xpl resolve` command: opens the workspace with `skipExplainerIndex` set, refuses `--write` on an index that does not match the working tree (unless `--allow-stale`), calls `reresolveExplainer` and prints the report. It saves the explainer only when `--write` is given.

nodes.label: reresolveExplainer
nodes.summary: Re-resolves every anchor of a copy of the explainer: rewrites each anchor's `resolved` cache, updates the span of moved ones and rebinds the copy to the new index. It returns the copy with a report of the counts per status, the drifted llm elements, the drifted elements it leaves to others and every missing anchor.

nodes.label: resolveWith
nodes.summary: Classifies one anchor against the current index and file text. `missing`: the file or symbol is gone; `ok` or `moved`: the stored hash still matches, at the expected lines or elsewhere in the symbol; `drifted`: the text changed and was not found.

nodes.label: searchSpan
nodes.summary: Looks for the stored hash inside the region it is given: first windows of the original length, then windows over the non-blank lines using prefix hashes. Candidates nearest to the expected start are tried first, and the second pass stops once a budget of prefix hashes is spent.

nodes.label: IndexModel
nodes.summary: The in-memory model of an index: lookups of files and symbols by path, and suggestions of similar files (`suggestFiles`) and symbols (`suggestSymbols`).

nodes.label: statusCommand.run
nodes.summary: The `xpl status` command, a read-only to-do list: what the views show without a summary, drifted elements (user-owned ones counted apart), missing anchors, broken references, stale edge overlays and queued viewer requests. It re-resolves the anchors itself with `reresolveExplainer`.

nodes.label: applyPatch
nodes.summary: Merges a patch into an explainer: it builds an `Applier` for the actor and runs the patch through it.

nodes.label: makeAnchor
nodes.summary: Builds a stored anchor from an input `{file, symbol?, span | find, role}`: a symbol-relative span (a `find` text becomes the span of the lines it touches), the hash of the normalized lines (the symbol's or file's hash for a whole-symbol anchor) and a `resolved` entry with status `ok`. It rejects unknown files or symbols with suggestions, `find` text that is missing or ambiguous, spans of blank lines and a `hash` that is no longer current.

edges.label: bin/xpl runs dist/xpl.mjs
edges.summary: The launcher bin/xpl builds the path of packages/cli/dist/xpl.mjs (or takes XPL_CLI) and imports it, which runs the CLI; build.ts writes that file from src/main.ts. The link is a file path, not an import statement.

edges.label: viewer page (dist/index.html)
edges.summary: The CLI takes the viewer as a built file: Vite writes one self-contained dist/index.html, build.ts copies it to dist/viewer.html, and readViewerHtml reads it (viewer.html next to the CLI bundle, else the viewer's own dist/index.html). `xpl bundle` and the `xpl view` server each call injectBundle to put the bundle into that page.

edges.label: HTTP /api (xpl view)
edges.summary: When the bundle names a server, the viewer's ServerApi fetches source files, PUTs edited views and tours and POSTs explain requests; `xpl view` names one (`/api`) and the CLI's server answers those routes in `handle`. The route strings are the contract between the two.

edges.label: applyPatch, injectBundle, …
edges.summary: The new, apply and bundle handlers call core's createExplainer, applyPatch and injectBundle; the CLI does the file reading and writing around them.

edges.label: buildIndex, writeIndex, …
edges.summary: `xpl index` calls the indexer's buildIndex and writeIndex. WorkingTree in repo.ts also calls discoverFiles, FileHasher and resolveCommitId to recompute the working tree's commit id and file hashes, and stalenessOf compares them with an existing index.

edges.label: hashText, splitLines, …
edges.summary: The hashes in an index follow core's hashText: FileHasher recomputes them with Node's native sha256, checks itself against hashText on a fixed sample and falls back to hashText if they differ. indexFile splits each file with core's splitLines and hashes it with FileHasher.

edges.label: parseBundle, deriveGraph, …
edges.summary: loadBundle has core parse the bundle with parseBundle, and deriveView has core derive the graph of a view with deriveGraph from the view and the model.

edges.label: pack.extract(ctx)
edges.summary: `indexFile` calls `pack.extract(parsed.ctx)` on whatever pack `packForFile` picks from the `languagePacks` registry, so build.ts does not name a concrete pack: for `.ts`, `.tsx` and `.js` files the call lands in `typescriptPack.extract` (the other packs are reached the same way), and the index has no reference from build.ts to typescript.ts.

edges.label: pack.resolveModule(spec, file, repo)
edges.summary: `Resolver.modules` asks the importing file's pack which repository files a module specifier names; for `.ts`, `.tsx` and `.js` files that is `resolveTypescriptModule`, which the pack object assigns by name (`resolveModule: resolveTypescriptModule`), so the index has no call from heuristic.ts to it.

edges.label: pack.classifySite(ctx, line, col)
edges.summary: `Mapper.classify` runs inside `input.withFile`, which parses the file and hands its pack to the callback; `pack.classifySite` then reaches the file's own pack (`typescriptPack.classifySite` for TypeScript and JavaScript), and the index has no reference from map.ts to typescript.ts.

edges.label: resolver.resolve(input)
edges.summary: `buildIndex` takes its resolvers from `preciseResolvers()` (or `opts.resolvers`) and calls `resolver.resolve(...)`; the three SCIP resolvers are in that registry because build.ts imports `./scip/index.js`, which calls `registerScipResolvers()` when it loads, so the index has no call from build.ts to them.

edges.label: command.run(ctx, args)
edges.summary: `dispatch` finds the command by name in the `COMMANDS` array and calls `command.run(ctx, args)` through the `CommandSpec` interface; `applyCommand` is listed in that array, so it is the object that call reaches, but no call edge points at `applyCommand.run`.

edges.label: throw CliError, then `error: ...`
edges.summary: A patch that is not valid JSON ends the command at `readPatch`: `parseJson` throws a `CliError`, `run()` in cli.ts catches whatever `dispatch` throws and hands it to `reportError`, which prints `error: <message>` on stderr (one JSON object on stdout with `--json`) and returns the error's exit code.

edges.label: applyPatch(...)
edges.summary: `run` passes the explainer, the patch, the index model, the working-tree text cache and the actor to `applyPatch`.

edges.label: loadExplainer / openWorkspace
edges.summary: `run` loads the explainer file and opens the workspace; the workspace's `model` and `texts` are what `applyPatch` is given.

edges.label: parseJson / atomicWrite
edges.summary: `readPatch` parses the patch with `parseJson`, and `run` writes the accepted result with `atomicWrite`.

edges.label: renderIssues / issueSummary
edges.summary: `run` prints every issue with `renderIssues` (one `severity path [id]: message` line each) and heads the issue list of a successful apply with `issueSummary` (`N errors, M warnings`).

edges.label: workingTreeReader / parseJson
edges.summary: `WorkingTree` reads files through `workingTreeReader`, and `readExplainerFile` parses the explainer file with `parseJson`.

edges.label: new TextCache(...)
edges.summary: `WorkingTree` builds a `TextCache` over the working-tree reader, and `openWorkspace` returns it as `texts`, the cache `run` passes to `applyPatch`.

edges.label: makeAnchor(...)
edges.summary: `Applier.anchors` builds each stored anchor with `makeAnchor`, giving it hints from the explainer's own whole-symbol anchors (`storedSymbolHints`) for its `Did you mean` candidates.

edges.label: validateExplainer(...)
edges.summary: `Applier.validate` runs `validateExplainer` in strict mode on the caller's explainer and on the merged copy.

edges.label: resolveWith(...)
edges.summary: `checkAnchors` calls `resolveWith` for each stored anchor to learn whether it is ok, moved, drifted or missing.

edges.label: normalizeLines / hashNormalized
edges.summary: `makeAnchor` hashes the trimmed non-blank lines of a span with these two functions, and `resolveWith` recomputes the same hash through `hashOf` when it re-checks the anchor.

edges.label: file / symbolAt / suggestSymbols
edges.summary: `makeAnchor` looks the file and symbol up in the index and, when one is not there, asks `suggestFiles` or `suggestSymbols` for the `Did you mean` candidates.

edges.label: state changed
edges.summary: After replacing the state, ViewerStore.set calls every listener in its `listeners` set; useViewerState in hooks.ts registers React's listener through useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.getState), which is how the components that read the state are told to render again. The listeners are stored callbacks, so no call edge leads from store.ts to hooks.ts.

edges.label: onCursor(from, to)
edges.summary: The update listener that createReadOnlyEditor installs calls handlers.onCursor with the lines the selection covers; EditorPane passes a handler that forwards them to store.setCursor(pane.file, from, to). The handler is a function stored in a field, so no call edge leads from editor.ts to EditorStack.tsx.

edges.label: resolveWith
edges.summary: Strict `xpl validate` classifies every anchor with the same `resolveWith`: drifted and missing ones are errors in strict mode and warnings in lenient mode, and the message says when the user owns the element, so an llm patch cannot repair it.

edges.label: makeAnchor
edges.summary: The anchors of an llm patch are rebuilt here from the current text, with a fresh hash and status `ok`; that rebuild is what clears drift.

edges.label: validateExplainer
edges.summary: The merged result is validated strictly before it is accepted: only problems the patch introduced or touched can reject it, and drift the user's own anchors already had stays a warning.

edges.label: new ViewerStore
edges.summary: main.tsx builds the store from the parsed bundle and the launch parameters read from the URL.

edges.label: getDerived
edges.summary: useDerived returns getDerived of the current state, so the components that call it read the same memoised Derived for one state.

edges.label: deriveGraph, repr
edges.summary: deriveView calls deriveGraph for a graph view; stubFocus and relatedIds call repr to find the box that stands for an element, and stubFocus asks derivedEdgeAnchors for the reference sites.

edges.label: codeFocus, reverse index
edges.summary: For the selection (diagram to code) derive.ts calls codeFocus and mergeFocusByFile; for the caret (code to diagram) it calls viewCandidates and buildReverseIndex once per view and then lookup for each line.

edges.label: deriveGraph, derivedEdgeAnchors
edges.summary: viewCandidates derives the view's graph when it is not handed one, and derivedFocus takes the reference sites and definitions of a derived edge from derivedEdgeAnchors when the view's graph does not have that edge.

edges.label: planStubs
edges.summary: deriveGraph reads the view's stub policy with resolveStubPolicy and hands the stub candidates it collected to planStubs, which decides which ghosts and stubs are drawn.

edges.label: expandStub, drillIn, collapse
edges.summary: The store's view edits call expandStub, drillIn and collapse, which return the view with a changed include list; stillShown calls deriveGraph to keep the selected ids that the edited view still draws.

edges.label: GraphView
edges.summary: For a graph view DiagramPane renders GraphView with the derived graph, the selection, the caret matches and the related ids.

edges.label: SequenceView
edges.summary: For a sequence view DiagramPane renders SequenceView with the view and the model instead of a derived graph, plus the selection, the caret matches and the related ids.

edges.label: layoutGraphFitting
edges.summary: GraphView's layout effect calls layoutGraphFitting; BoxShape also calls badgeWidth to size the kind badge of a box.

edges.label: click, drillIn, expandStub
edges.summary: A click on a box or an edge calls store.click and a click on the empty canvas calls clearSelection; a double-click on a box calls drillIn and a click on a ghost of one element calls expandStub, both skipped while presenting.

edges.label: click
edges.summary: A click on a step or a lifeline calls store.click, and a click on the empty canvas calls clearSelection.

edges.label: createReadOnlyEditor, applyFocus

concepts.label: Language packs
concepts.summary: A language pack has three jobs: `extract(ctx)` turns one parsed file into plain facts (symbol drafts, reference sites, import bindings, type facts and exports); `classifySite(ctx, line, col)` says which kind of site the identifier at a position is (the SCIP mapper uses it); `resolveModule(spec, fromFile, repo)` lists the repository files a module specifier can name (the heuristic resolver and the SCIP mapper use it). Six packs are registered: typescript (TypeScript, TSX and JavaScript), python, go, and the config packs yaml, json and toml, which have `refs: "none"`.
concepts.detail:
A pack works on one parsed file at a time and hands back plain facts. By contract it keeps no tree-sitter nodes (the tree is freed right after `extract`), does not assign symbol ids, `~N` suffixes, hashes or parents, and does not resolve references: `assembleSymbols` and the heuristic resolver do that.

- Positions are 1-based, inclusive lines and columns, with columns in UTF-16 code units.
- The receiver of a member access is spelled `"this"` (TypeScript `this`, Python `self` and `cls`, Go receiver names); TypeScript `super` stays `"super"`.
- `refs` is `"heuristic"` when `extract` produces sites and `"none"` for config formats; `packageScope` says whether a top-level name is visible per `file` (TypeScript, Python) or per `directory` (Go).
- The config packs (yaml, json, toml) return mapping keys as symbols of kind `key`, addressed by their dotted path (a per-file cap applies), and no sites.
- The Go pack declares `inferRefs`, an optional pass after the heuristic resolver that infers `implements` references (a Go type implements an interface by having its methods).

- `--commit` wins over everything; `validateCommitId` allows letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-` because the id is part of the file name `index-<commit>.json`.
- The short HEAD is used only when the root is the git top level and `git status --porcelain=v1 --ignore-submodules=all -- . :(exclude).explainer` prints nothing, so changes under `.explainer/` do not make the tree dirty (file discovery skips `.explainer/` too).
- Otherwise `workingTreeId` hashes the sorted `path\0hash` lines with SHA-256 and keeps `wt-` plus 10 hex characters. The hashes are the whitespace-insensitive file hashes from `FileHasher` and the paths are relative to the root, so the id is deterministic and does not depend on where the directory lives.
- A root that is a subdirectory of a work tree gets a `wt-` id even when the tree is clean.

concepts.label: Reference sites
concepts.summary: A site is a name mention that a pack records without resolving it: `kind` is `call`, `import`, `extends`, `implements`, `type-ref`, `write` or `read`, `name` is the last segment and `qualifier` the receiver chain (`this.pool.lease()` gives ["this", "pool"] and `lease`), and `site` is its span; the framework later takes the innermost symbol around the span as the reference's `from`. In the TypeScript pack `Extractor.scan` walks the tree once and hands calls, `new`, assignments, heritage clauses, type references and JSX to their handlers, and `Extractor.onReads` adds the `read` sites.
concepts.detail:
- `call`: `name(...)`, `recv.name(...)`, `new Name(...)` and JSX components; the site is the whole call, or only the callee when the call spans more than 10 lines (`SITE_MAX_LINES`, `callSpan`).
- `import`: an import without bindings (`import "./x"`, `import("./x")`, `require("./x")`); imports that bind names become `ImportBinding`s, which the resolver turns into `import` references, or `type-ref` when the binding is type-only.
- `extends` and `implements` are heritage clauses; `type-ref` is a name in a type position.
- `write`: an assignment or update of a field or module variable; the site is the whole assignment, or only its target when it spans more than 10 lines.
- `read`: a use of a variable or field that is not a call or a write; locals and parameters are left out, and a bare name counts only when the file declares it as a variable or imports it and no enclosing scope binds it (`Extractor.onReads`).

concepts.label: Heuristic references
concepts.summary: The heuristic resolver turns each reference site (call, import, extends, implements, type-ref, write, read) into a reference by resolving its qualifier and name: lexical scopes and the file's top-level symbols first, then import bindings through `resolveModule` (following re-exports and star exports, and for Go the other files of the package directory), and a qualified name through the type of its receiver. Only when a call or write has a receiver of completely unknown type does it pick a class named like the receiver that has the member, dropping the site when the best matches tie; sites it cannot resolve are dropped.
concepts.detail:
- `Resolver.run` goes file by file: import bindings, re-exports, then sites.
- Every reference is marked `resolution: "heuristic"`; a reference whose `from` equals its `to` is dropped and a repeated (from, to, kind, site) is kept once (`Resolver.add`).
- `WANT` filters candidates by site kind: a `read` points only at a variable, a call never at an interface, a type alias or a config key.
- The name fallback ranks classes: the same file, then a class the file imports, then the same directory, then any other; a tie at the best rank drops the site (`Resolver.nameMatch`, `Resolver.rank`).
- Receivers whose type is known but lies outside the repository (`Map`, `Promise`, an npm import) are opaque: nothing is guessed for them.

- A language with no described file is left out of `preciseLanguages` (no tool name); when that holds for every language the resolver covers, the resolver counts as failed: a warning in `auto`, an error in `require`.

concepts.summary: A patch object is upserted by id into the clone: a new id needs its required fields, an existing one is shallow-merged (fields sent replace, fields omitted stay, arrays and objects replace whole), and `null` clears a field only when its spec lists it as nullable (for example `summary`, `detail`, `members`, `hidden`, `layout`), otherwise it is an error. `includeAdd` / `includeRemove` and `stepsUpdate` are patch-only fields that edit a view's `include`, or single steps, without resending the whole list.

concepts.label: The user's edits win
concepts.summary: For the llm actor, an existing element, view or tour with `origin: "user"` is skipped whole with a `protected` warning, a field listed in `provenance.userFields` keeps the user's value (even against `null`), and `remove` skips what the user authored or edited. `--actor user` and the viewer's `PUT /api/views|tours` apply patches as `user`: an edit of an llm element records the changed fields in its `userFields`, and a new element becomes `origin: "user"`. When a patch touched only protected content nothing changes and the CLI exits 1.
concepts.detail:
- **Whole element:** `skipUserOwned` skips an existing element, view or tour with `origin: "user"`.
- **One field:** `mergeExisting` reads `provenance.userFields` into `protectedKeys`, and `convertFields` skips those keys before it looks at `null`.
- **View lists:** `includeRemove` and `stepsUpdate` are skipped when the user edited `include` or `steps`; `includeAdd` still applies.
- **Removal:** `remove` skips a user-authored item, anything that carries `userFields`, and single steps of a view whose `steps` the user edited.
- **New elements** get `origin` of the actor, and an llm patch cannot ask for `origin: "user"`. A tour without provenance counts as the llm's.
- **Validation:** an old anchor problem on a touched element whose anchors the user owns (`origin: "user"`, or `anchors` / `steps` in `userFields`, which is how a tour's step code is locked) stays a warning, since an llm patch cannot repair it.
- **CLI:** a result that is ok, changed nothing and has `protected` warnings is refused with exit 1 and advice; when only part of the patch was skipped the exit code stays 0 and the output ends with `skipped as protected (...)`.

concepts.label: What a rejection does
concepts.summary: Any error left after the merge and the validation makes `fail()` return the caller's untouched explainer with `changed: []`, so nothing is written: the CLI prints `rejected: N errors, nothing was applied to <file>` with every issue and exits 1. Validation keeps an error only if the patch introduced or touched it, so a problem already sitting in an untouched part becomes one warning instead of blocking every later patch.
concepts.detail:
- **Merge errors:** an unknown field or patch key, a wrong type, a missing required field, an unknown id, a failed anchor, a changed `kind` / `type`, an id used twice: each is recorded with `error(...)` while the merge goes on.
- **Validation errors:** the merged copy is validated strictly; errors of untouched parts collapse into one warning (`N existing validation error(s) ... were ignored`).
- **Result:** `fail()` returns `{ok: false, explainer: input, issues, changed: []}`, so the CLI's `write` is false and the file is not touched.
- **Output:** `rejected: N errors, nothing was applied to <file> (patch from <label>)`, one line per issue, exit code 1; with `--json`, `ok: false`, `applied: false` and `error: "patch rejected: N errors, nothing applied"`.
- **Fatal errors** (invalid JSON, an unreadable file, an unknown explainer, no index) are `CliError`s thrown before `applyPatch` is reached: `error: ...` on stderr, an empty stdout, exit code 1.
- **A refusal, not a rejection:** a patch whose every change was user-protected exits 1 too (see the user-protection concept).

concepts.label: Innermost wins
concepts.summary: When several elements cover the line under the caret, those whose range spans the fewest lines win, and elements tied on that size are all returned, sorted by id; an element with several ranges around the line counts by its smallest one.
concepts.detail:
The rule lives in `lookup`, built by `buildReverseIndex`: for one line it keeps, per candidate, the smallest range that contains the line, takes the smallest of those sizes and returns every candidate of that size.

- A step's call site (a line or two) beats a lifeline or a definition that contains it, so a caret on that line lights up the step, not the lifeline.
- A symbol beats its file, because the file's range is the whole file.
- A selection of several lines looks every line up (at most 400) and lights up the union, sorted by id.

The candidates are what the current view shows plus every concept, so the same caret can light up different elements in another view.

- **Where a stub comes from.** deriveGraph lifts both ends of each reference; when only one end has a box, `addStub` records a candidate towards the highest ancestor of the outside end that holds no node of the view (`ghostTarget`).
- **Folding.** In mode `top`, `foldKey` gives a symbol whose file is shown in part, and such a file itself, the key `rest:file:<path>`, so the outside symbols of one file become one ghost.
- **Cap.** The ghosts are ranked by the references that lead to them (ties by key); beyond `max` (default 8) they become `ghost:more:in` or `ghost:more:out`, labelled with the number of elements they stand for.
- **Expanding.** Clicking a ghost that stands for one element adds it to the view's `include` (`store.expandStub`); a folded ghost opens a menu of what it stands for, and nothing happens in Present. Selecting the stub itself shows the crossing reference sites in the code.

concepts.label: Hashes of normalized text
concepts.summary: An anchor stores the hash of its lines after every line is trimmed and blank lines are dropped (`sha256:` and 12 hex digits), and resolving compares those hashes, not the text itself. Re-indenting, trailing spaces, CRLF line endings and blank lines therefore leave the hash as it was (at most the anchor is `moved`), while any other edit to a line, spacing inside it included, gives a different hash.
concepts.detail:
**What is hashed.** `normalizeLines` trims every line, drops the ones that are empty afterwards and joins the rest with `\n`; `hashNormalized` keeps the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of that string (`hashText` does both steps). Only the ends of a line are trimmed, so `a  =  b` and `a = b` hash differently.

**Where it is used.**
- Span anchors: `makeAnchor` stores the hash of the anchored lines, `hashOf` hashes the lines at the expected place, and `resolveWith` compares the two (regen:7).
- Whole-symbol and whole-file anchors: the index stores a hash of the same kind for its symbols and files (the indexer's `FileHasher` trims and drops blank lines the same way), and `resolveWith` compares it with the anchor's (regen:8).
- Finding moved code: `searchSpan` drops the blank lines, then `normalizedPrefixHashes` hashes the prefixes of the non-blank lines from a start line (up to the length of the original span) with one running digest, so code that gained or lost blank lines is still found (regen:10).

**What it buys.** Formatting churn leaves an anchor `ok`, or `moved` when its lines shifted; the regeneration tests re-indent, add trailing spaces, switch to CRLF and insert blank lines without a drift. An edit to the anchored lines themselves gives a different hash, so the anchor drifts (unless the old text still sits elsewhere in the symbol), and `resolve` keeps the stored hash, so reverting the edit makes the anchor `ok` again.

concepts.label: Symbol-relative spans
concepts.summary: A span is stored as 0-based line offsets from the first line of its symbol (from line 1 of the file when the anchor has no symbol), next to the hash of those lines. When code above the symbol shifts it, the offsets still fit and the anchor is `moved` with no search; when lines are added or removed inside the symbol, the anchored text is searched for in that symbol only and the anchor gets a new span.
concepts.detail:
**Where the offsets come from.** `makeAnchor` turns a `span`, or the lines a `find` text touches, into offsets from the symbol's first line (`base`) and hashes those lines. `resolveWith` adds the `base` of the symbol as it is in the current index, so a symbol that moves as a whole takes its anchors along.

**What happens when the code moves.**
- Only the symbol moved (lines added above it): the hash matches at the new `base + span`, the status is `moved` and the stored span is unchanged; the Python and Go regeneration tests add a method above `dispatch` and see exactly that.
- Lines added or removed inside the symbol, above or within the span: the hash no longer matches at the expected lines, so `searchSpan` looks for it inside the symbol, nearest match first, and the anchor gets a new span (regen:9 to regen:12).
- The symbol got shorter: the expected range is clamped into the symbol (`clampRange`) before it is hashed.

**Limits.** A span is only re-found while its text is unchanged; otherwise the anchor is `drifted` (regen:13). A symbol that is renamed or removed makes it `missing` (regen:4).

concepts.label: User edits survive re-explanation
concepts.summary: What the user writes is recorded in provenance (`origin: "user"` for what they create, `userFields` for fields they change on an llm element), and the later steps read it: `resolve` reports user-owned drift apart, `status` counts it as 'ask the user', and an llm patch skips user-authored items, keeps the fields in `userFields` and does not remove what carries them.
concepts.detail:
**How it is recorded.** A patch applied with actor `user` marks the elements, views and tours it creates `origin: "user"`, and adds the fields it changes on an existing llm or static element to that element's `provenance.userFields` (`newProvenance`, `mergeExisting`). The viewer's saves take this path: the view server applies `PUT /api/views/<id>` and `/api/tours/<id>` as actor `user`.

**What each step does with it.**
1. `xpl resolve` (`reresolveExplainer`): drifted anchors of `user` or static owners go to `driftedOther`, printed as 'left alone'; a drifted llm element carries its `userFields`, printed as `[keep userFields: ...]`. Moved anchors of every owner still get their coordinates rewritten: only the span changes, the hash does not.
2. `xpl status` (`driftCounts`): drift the user owns is counted apart, `N drifted (K user-owned: ask the user)`: all of `driftedOther`, plus llm elements whose `anchors` (for a step: its view's `steps`) are in `userFields`.
3. `xpl apply` as actor `llm` (`Applier`): an existing element, view or tour with origin `user` is skipped whole (`skipUserOwned`); fields in `userFields` are kept (`convertFields`); for a view, `includeRemove` and `stepsUpdate` are skipped when `include` or `steps` are protected while `includeAdd` still adds; a `remove` of anything user-authored or carrying `userFields` is skipped; and the patch cannot create user-authored items.
4. Validation: drift on anchors the user owns is flagged `userLocked`, the message says to tell the user or use `--actor user`, and drift that was already there does not block an llm patch that touches the element.
5. Exit code: when every change of a patch was skipped as protected, `xpl apply` exits 1 and names the ids instead of reporting success.

The skips are warnings with code `protected`. The advice `xpl apply` prints is to put new content in a new view or new elements, grow a curated view with `includeAdd`, ask the user, and never re-create an element under another id to replace theirs.

views.title: From a repository to a viewer: index, new, apply, bundle, load

scope.question: What happens, command by command, from indexing a repository to the viewer showing an explainer?

steps.label: xpl index: buildIndex({ root, precise, commit })
steps.summary: `xpl index` is where the skill's workflow starts. `dispatch` runs the command's handler, which calls buildIndex with the repo root, the precise mode and an optional commit id. buildIndex discovers the files, parses each one once, resolves references heuristically and, unless precise is `off`, lets a precise resolver replace them file by file; writeIndex then saves `.explainer/index-<commit>.json` and keeps `index-*.json` in `.explainer/.gitignore`.

steps.label: xpl new: createExplainer({ title, repoName, index, indexPath })
steps.summary: `xpl new <name>` opens the index and detects the repository name, then calls createExplainer, which returns an empty explainer bound to that index: the schema tag, title, repo, index path and commit, and empty nodes, edges, concepts, views and tours. The handler writes it to `.explainer/<name>.explainer.json`.

steps.label: xpl apply: applyPatch(explainer, patch, index, texts, { actor })
steps.summary: `xpl apply <name> patch.json` loads the explainer and the patch, opens the index and the source texts, and calls applyPatch as actor `llm` (or `user` with `--actor user`). When a check fails, applyPatch returns the explainer as it was, together with the issues it collected. The handler writes the file when the result is ok, it is not a dry run and something changed; a rejected patch prints its issues, writes nothing and exits 1.

steps.label: xpl bundle: injectBundle(html, bundle)
steps.summary: `xpl bundle -o out.html` reads the viewer page, chooses which source files and how much of the index to embed, and wraps them with the explainer into one bundle object. injectBundle then puts the bundle's JSON into the page as a `<script id="xpl-data">` element (`<` escaped), and the handler writes the page to the output path. `xpl view` calls injectBundle the same way for each request to `/`.

steps.label: page opens: parseBundle(text)
steps.summary: When the page opens, main.tsx calls loadBundle: it looks up the `<script id="xpl-data">` element, has core's parseBundle parse its text (a wrong `schema` throws) and checks that the bundle has an explainer and an index. main.tsx then builds a ViewerStore from the bundle and renders the App, or shows the error message when loading failed.

steps.label: draw: deriveGraph(view, model)
steps.summary: To draw a graph view, the viewer's deriveView passes the view and the model to core's deriveGraph. deriveGraph builds the arrows from the index's references, aggregated per pair of boxes and filtered by the view's edge kinds and excludeFiles, overlays the explainer's stored edges, and works out the stubs (edges that leave the view). deriveView also builds a reverse index over the view's elements.

scope.question: How does `xpl index` turn a repository into a symbol index?

steps.label: buildIndex({ root, precise, commit })
steps.summary: `indexCommand.run` passes the repository root, the `--precise` mode (default `auto`) and the optional `--commit` override to `buildIndex`, which builds the index; the command writes the result afterwards.

steps.label: detectGit(root)
steps.summary: Asks git whether the root is inside a work tree (`git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree --show-toplevel`) and whether it is the top-level directory; the answer is undefined when git is missing or the root is not in a work tree.

steps.label: discoverFiles(root, { git, languages })
steps.summary: Lists candidate paths with `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard` in a git work tree, else walks the directory (skipping dot-directories and build or dependency directories such as `node_modules`, `dist` and `vendor`); it then drops `.explainer/`, `node_modules` and `.git` paths, lockfiles, files over 1 MiB and files with a NUL byte in the first 8 KiB, and returns the rest sorted by path, each with a language chosen by extension (`text` when unknown).

steps.label: indexFile(discovered, pool, ...)
steps.summary: For each discovered file, `indexFile` reads the text (a file that vanished or cannot be read is skipped), splits it into lines and builds the `IndexedFile` record (path, language, hash, line count); a file whose language has no pack (plain `text`) stops there and has no symbols.

steps.label: hashFile()
steps.summary: `FileHasher` hashes the whole file as `sha256:` plus the first 12 hex characters of the SHA-256 of its trimmed, non-blank lines; the value is stored as `IndexedFile.hash`.

steps.label: pack.extract(ctx)
steps.summary: The text is parsed with the tree-sitter grammar the pack names for the file's language, and `extract` turns the syntax tree into plain facts: symbol drafts (path, kind, range), reference sites, import bindings, type facts and exports. The TypeScript pack's `Extractor.run` visits the statements for symbols and imports and then scans the tree for sites; the Python, Go, YAML, JSON and TOML packs implement the same `extract`.

steps.label: assembleSymbols(path, lines, drafts, hasher)
steps.summary: Turns the drafts into `IndexedSymbol`s: they are sorted by position, each gets the id `<file>#<path>`, a path used more than once is numbered in source order (`x`, `x~2`, `x~3`), the range becomes whole lines, and `parentPath` is resolved to the draft with that path that contains it (else the nearest one before it).

steps.label: hashRange(range)
steps.summary: A symbol's `hash` is `hasher.hashRange(range)`: its lines are trimmed, blank ones dropped, and the first 12 hex characters of their SHA-256 are kept, so re-indenting or adding blank lines does not change it.

scope.question: How does `xpl index` turn a repository into a symbol index?

steps.label: resolveHeuristic({ files, entries, lookup, repo })
steps.summary: Every reference site the packs collected is looked up through scopes, import bindings, the declared types of receivers and, as a last resort for calls and writes, a name match on the receiver, and becomes a reference with `resolution: "heuristic"`; sites that cannot be resolved are dropped. Only files of packs with `refs: "heuristic"` (TypeScript and JavaScript, Python, Go) take part, and `inferPackRefs` then adds what a pack infers across files (Go's implicit interfaces).

steps.label: pack.resolveModule(spec, file, repo)
steps.summary: To follow an import the resolver asks the importing file's pack which repository files a module specifier names: the TypeScript pack probes extensions and `index` files for relative specifiers, gives no file for `node:` or URL specifiers, and treats a bare specifier as external unless the repository defines it itself (tsconfig `paths`, workspace packages, package.json `imports`).

steps.label: resolver.resolve(input)
steps.summary: For each registered resolver whose languages still have heuristic references and no precise tool yet, `buildIndex` calls `resolve` with the root, files, symbols, a symbol lookup and helpers to read and parse files; with `--precise off` no resolver runs. The SCIP resolvers (scip-typescript for TypeScript, TSX and JavaScript, scip-python, scip-go) run an external indexer and map its output (next view).

steps.label: PreciseOutput { refs, tool, describedFiles }
steps.summary: The resolver returns the precise references, the tool name and version, and `describedFiles`, the files its index described; `buildIndex` keeps only the references that start in files of the languages it asked about.

steps.label: replace the references of described files
steps.summary: Per file, not per language: the heuristic references of each file the tool described (`describedFiles`, plus any file it produced a reference for) are replaced by the precise ones, while the other files of a language that became precise keep their heuristic references and are counted in `keptHeuristicFiles`, which becomes `heuristicFiles` in the language summary.

steps.label: warn and keep heuristic references (or throw)
steps.summary: If the tool cannot run, fails, or described none of the files of its languages, `auto` records a warning and those languages keep their heuristic references; `--precise require` throws instead, so the build fails.

steps.label: resolveCommitId({ commit, git, files, root })
steps.summary: The id is the `--commit` value if given; else the first 7 characters of HEAD when the root is the git top level and only `.explainer/` differs from HEAD; else `wt-` plus the first 10 hex characters of a SHA-256 over the sorted `path\0hash` lines of the indexed files.

steps.label: { index, warnings }
steps.summary: `buildIndex` returns the `SymbolIndex` (schema, commit, tool string, per-language summary, root, files, symbols and references) together with the warnings collected on the way.

steps.label: writeIndex(root, index)
steps.summary: `writeIndex` writes `.explainer/index-<commit>.json` pretty-printed, through a temporary file and a rename, and makes sure `.explainer/.gitignore` lists `index-*.json`; the command then prints the warnings and one line per language whose `refs:` part `describeRefs` builds (`precise <described>/<files> (<tool>), <n> heuristic` when some files kept heuristic references).

views.title: xpl index (3/3): inside a SCIP resolver

scope.question: How do the SCIP precise resolvers replace heuristic references per described file?

steps.label: resolver.resolve(input)
steps.summary: The scip-typescript resolver covers `typescript`, `tsx` and `javascript`; its `resolve` runs the tool and hands the output to `finish`. `scipPythonResolver` (Python) and `scipGoResolver` (Go) have the same shape around `runScipPython` and `runScipGo`.

steps.label: runScipTypescript(root, files, cfg)
steps.summary: For TypeScript and JavaScript it runs `npx --yes @sourcegraph/scip-typescript@<pinned version> index --cwd <root> --output <tmp>.scip` on the repository's tsconfig and jsconfig projects, indexes any file no project covers through a generated tsconfig, and decodes each `.scip` file into a `ScipSource`. scip-python runs `npx` once for the whole repository and scip-go runs `go run` once per go.mod.

steps.label: runTool("npx", args), readIndex(output)
steps.summary: The tool runs as a child process with a timeout (10 minutes unless `XPL_SCIP_TIMEOUT_MS` sets another); a start failure, a timeout or a non-zero exit becomes an error naming the tool, and the `.scip` file it wrote is read and decoded.

steps.label: mapScip({ root, languages, files, lookup, ..., sources })
steps.summary: `Mapper.run` loads the SCIP documents that are indexed files, collects the definition occurrences, turns each other occurrence whose definition is a symbol of the index into a reference from the innermost symbol at that place to that definition, and adds `implements` references from the tool's implementation relationships.

steps.label: pack.classifySite(ctx, line, col)
steps.summary: For the occurrences of a document that have a target, the mapper parses the file once through `withFile` and asks its pack, for each occurrence, what kind of site sits at that position (call, import, extends, implements, type-ref, write or read) and how far it extends; when the pack does not classify it, the mapper falls back on the SCIP roles and on whether the target is a type.

steps.label: MapResult { refs, described, uncovered }
steps.summary: `mapScip` returns the references, `described` (the indexed files of the covered languages that a SCIP document described) and `uncovered` (the ones no document described).

steps.label: warnUncovered(input, tool, uncovered)
steps.summary: Files no SCIP document described are named in one warning (five examples at most, none from `node_modules`, `vendor` or `testdata` directories); their references stay heuristic.

steps.label: PreciseOutput { refs, tool, describedFiles }
steps.summary: `finish` returns `refs`, `tool` and `describedFiles`; the tool name comes from the SCIP index metadata (`toolName@toolVersion`) and falls back to the pinned version when the index carries none.

views.title: How xpl apply merges, anchors, validates and writes a patch

scope.question: How does a patch become validated, hash-checked anchors, and what happens when it is rejected?

steps.label: applyPatch(explainer, patch, model, texts, {actor})
steps.summary: After loading the explainer and reading the patch (a JSON syntax error is a `CliError` thrown here, before core is called) and opening the workspace, `run` hands the explainer, the patch, the index model, the working-tree text cache and the actor (`llm` by default) to `applyPatch`. That builds an `Applier`, whose constructor keeps the input and makes a deep clone `work` that the edits go into.

steps.label: upsertElement / upsertView / upsertTour
steps.summary: `run` records an unknown top-level key as an error, then upserts nodes, edges, concepts, views and tours, in that order, into `work`: a new id is created (with its required fields), an existing one is merged, and an existing element, view or tour that the user authored is skipped with a `protected` warning when the actor is `llm`. `title` and `remove` follow, and `validate()` runs after them even when an upsert failed.

steps.label: mergeExisting(...) / convertFields(...)
steps.summary: `mergeExisting` refuses to change a node's `kind` or a view's `type`, takes the fields in `provenance.userFields` as protected (llm actor only), and asks `convertFields` to turn each field of the patch into stored form: `null` marks the field to clear, a protected field is skipped with a `protected` warning, the rest is set (anchors are built by `makeAnchor`, next). The result is the existing element cloned with those fields replaced whole, arrays and objects included, and the cleared ones deleted; when nothing differs the element is left as it was and is not listed in `changed`.

steps.label: makeAnchor(input, index, texts, options)
steps.summary: Each AnchorInput of an `anchors` array (an element's, a sequence step's, a tour step's `code`, a `stepsUpdate` entry's) goes through `makeAnchor` with the index model, the working-tree text cache and hints taken from the explainer's own whole-symbol anchors. It checks the input's shape, then the file and symbol in the index: an unknown one fails, with `Did you mean` candidates when there are any (files, or up to 3 symbols printed as an id and as anchor fields).

steps.label: locateText(lines, find)
steps.summary: With `find`, `locateText` searches only the symbol's lines (the whole file when there is no symbol): one exact hit, or failing that one ignoring whitespace differences, becomes the span of the lines it touches; no hit, an empty text or several hits (the error lists their offsets) are errors.

steps.label: normalizeLines + hashNormalized
steps.summary: The range is the symbol's first line plus the span offsets (a span past the symbol's last line is refused). Its lines are trimmed and blank ones dropped, a span of blank lines only is refused, and the hash is `sha256:` plus the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the rest, so leading or trailing whitespace and blank lines do not affect it; an anchor without a span takes the index's hash of the symbol (or file).

steps.label: {ok: true, anchor} | {ok: false, error}
steps.summary: A built anchor holds file, symbol, span, role, `hash` and `resolved: {commit, range, status: "ok"}` (a `hash` given in the input must equal the current one, else it is refused as stale). On a failure `Applier.anchors` records the message at `<path>[i]` with code `anchor-invalid`, remembers the element in `anchorFailures` and still returns the anchors that did build, so the rest of the element is still checked.

steps.label: applyIncludeOps / applyStepUpdates
steps.summary: After the fields, a graph view's `includeRemove` then `includeAdd` edit the merged `include` (ids not in it are appended), and a sequence view's `stepsUpdate` merges each entry into the step with that id: its `anchors` replace the step's, `null` clears `summary` or `edge`, an unknown step id is an error. When the user edited `include` or `steps`, `includeRemove` and `stepsUpdate` are skipped with a `protected` warning; `includeAdd` still applies.

steps.label: validateExplainer(input | work, index, texts, {mode: "strict"})
steps.summary: `Applier.validate` runs the strict validator twice: on the caller's explainer, to know which issues were there already, and on `work`, passing as `assumeIds` the ids of the elements, views and tours that failed to build so that one failure is not reported again at every reference to it. The validator then walks the whole explainer: nodes, edges, concepts, views and tours.

steps.label: resolveWith(anchor, index, texts)
steps.summary: For each stored anchor, `checkAnchors` calls `resolveWith`, which recomputes the hash of what is there now (the text at a span's range; the index's hash of the symbol or file when there is no span) and compares it with the stored one: equal is `ok` (`moved` when the lines are not where `resolved` says), different is `drifted` unless a span's text is found elsewhere in the symbol (then `moved`), and a vanished file or symbol is `missing`. In strict mode drifted and missing are errors; in lenient mode they are warnings.

steps.label: Issue[]
steps.summary: `Applier.validate` keeps an error when the patch introduced it (the caller's own explainer did not already have the same issue) or when it sits on an element the patch touched, and rewrites its path to point into the patch. The other errors collapse into one warning, and (llm actor) an old anchor problem on a touched element whose anchors the user owns stays a warning.

steps.label: ApplyResult {ok, explainer, issues, changed}
steps.summary: When any error is left, `fail()` returns `{ok: false, explainer: input, issues, changed: []}`: the caller's own object, which was never edited because the edits went into the clone. Otherwise the result is `ok: true` with `work`, the issues (warnings only) and the unique ids that changed.

steps.label: atomicWrite(path, jsonFile(result.explainer))
steps.summary: Only when `write` holds (result ok, not `--dry-run`, at least one id changed) is the merged explainer serialised as indented JSON and written to a temp file next to the target, which is then renamed over it; the temp file is removed if either step fails. This happens before anything is printed.

steps.label: rejected: N errors, nothing was applied
steps.summary: When `result.ok` is false nothing has been written: the command prints `rejected: N errors, nothing was applied to <file> (patch from <label>)` and one `severity path [id]: message` line per issue, then returns exit code 1 (with `--json`, one object with `ok: false`, `applied: false`, the issues and an `error`). A result that is ok but changed nothing because every change was user-protected is refused the same way, naming the protected ids and what to do.

scope.question: How does a view become boxes and arrows on screen, each with the id a click and a caret match use?

steps.label: useDerived()
steps.summary: DiagramPane asks for the derived state. getDerived derives the view the first time and again when the view id changed or the explainer's index, nodes, edges, concepts or views did, by calling deriveView.

steps.label: deriveGraph(view, model)
steps.summary: deriveView calls deriveGraph for a graph view only. Each reference of the shown kinds is lifted to the boxes that stand for its two ends: two different, unnested boxes give a derived edge, one end without a box gives a stub. Stored edges are laid over the derived ones, hidden ids are removed, and planStubs picks the ghosts to draw.

steps.label: <GraphView graph={derived.view.graph} ... />

steps.summary: Each anchor is judged on its own, from what it stores (file, symbol, span, hash and the range of the last resolve) and from the current index and file text. `resolveAnchor` is the exported wrapper that builds the index model and text cache and calls the same function.

steps.label: symbolAt(file, symbol)
steps.summary: A file that is no longer in the index, or a symbol path that is not in it any more, makes the anchor `missing` at once; the anchor is not retargeted and keeps the range of its last resolve (0-0 when it had none).

steps.label: suggestSymbols(file, symbol, 4, hint)
steps.summary: `describeVanished` builds the reason: for a span anchor it first searches the whole file for the anchored text and names the symbol that now holds it, with its anchor fields and new span. It then lists up to three `suggestSymbols` candidates: an identical body first (whole-symbol anchors carry their old size and hash as the hint), then a same-parent sibling with a similar name or the one of the old size, then the same name elsewhere, with test files last.

steps.label: missing

anchors.symbol: 4_ Queue_ack and its call are deleted.marks the Queue_ack concept's anchor missing and lists it with the reason

steps.summary: The result is `missing` plus the reason text. `reresolveExplainer` lists every missing anchor whatever its owner's origin; the anchor stays in the explainer with its last range, and the report says to fix or drop it explicitly.

steps.label: hashOf(lines, expected)
steps.summary: The expected place is the symbol's current first line plus the stored offsets, clamped into the symbol. Its lines are trimmed, blank lines dropped and the rest hashed (`hashOf`, through `normalizeLines` and `hashNormalized`), and a hash equal to the stored one means the text is unchanged.

anchors.symbol: 1_ five comment lines above Runner_dispatch.moves every anchor inside dispatch by five lines; spans and text are unchanged
other edits.formatting only (CRLF, re-indenting, trailing spaces) changes nothing: not even a move

steps.summary: Matching text is `ok`, or `moved` when its lines differ from the range cached by the last resolve (for instance code added above the symbol, whose offsets still fit). A whole-symbol or whole-file anchor is compared the same way, by the hash the index holds for the symbol or file.

steps.summary: When the hash differs at the expected lines, the symbol's own lines are searched for it (the whole file if the anchor has no symbol). Candidates are tried nearest to the expected start first, a tie goes to the earlier line, and the first match wins.

steps.label: normalizedPrefixHashes(nbText, p, rawLen)
steps.summary: The first pass tries windows of the original length; the second drops blank lines, tries each non-blank line as a start and gets the hashes of all prefixes up to `rawLen` lines from one running SHA-256. A prefix whose hash equals the stored one is a match even if blank lines were added or removed inside the span.

steps.label: { start, end }
steps.summary: A match comes back as the first and last matching line (in the second pass a non-blank line at each end); with no match it returns `undefined`, and the second pass also gives up once its count of computed hashes passes `MAX_SEARCH_OPS`.

steps.label: reresolveExplainer(loaded.explainer, ws.model, ws.texts)
steps.summary: `xpl status` calls `reresolveExplainer` itself, on the index the explainer is bound to (`chooseIndexFile` prefers it when `skipExplainerIndex` is not set), and turns the report into its to-do list. After `xpl index`, `xpl resolve --write` is what moves that binding to the new index.

steps.label: applyPatch(loaded.explainer, patch, ws.model, ws.texts, { actor })
steps.summary: `xpl apply` takes the actor from `--actor` (`llm` by default) and runs the patch through `applyPatch`, which builds an `Applier` for that actor and calls its `run`. The actor is what the rest of the sequence turns on: it is the `llm` actor that user-owned content holds back.

steps.label: skipUserOwned(existing, id, path)
steps.summary: For an element, view or tour that already exists, an llm actor first checks `provenance.origin`: `user` means the whole item is skipped with a `protected` warning. `upsertElement`, `upsertView` and `upsertTour` each call it before merging.

steps.label: convertFields(kind, raw, path, id, protectedKeys)

steps.summary: When the actor is `llm`, the fields the patch sends for an existing element are merged one by one, except those listed in the element's `provenance.userFields`: each of them is skipped with 'was edited by the user and is kept as it is'. So the user's summary, anchors, `include` or `steps` stay while the other fields are updated.

steps.label: makeAnchor(input, index, texts, options)

anchors.symbol: all five edits in one second commit.Claude re-explains: dispatch:3 is ok again, the user's summary is kept, the user concept is skipped

steps.summary: The anchors of a field that is not protected are rebuilt from the current text: a fresh hash, the lines they resolve to now and status `ok`; a `hash` sent along must equal the current one or the patch is rejected as stale. That rebuild is what clears drift: on an anchor, `reresolveExplainer` rewrites only `resolved` and, for a moved one, `span`, never the stored hash.

steps.label: remove(removals)
steps.summary: A `remove` in the patch is skipped with a `protected` warning for an element, view or tour that is user-authored or carries `userFields`, and for a step of a view whose `steps` the user edited.

steps.label: validateExplainer(work, index, texts, { mode: "strict" })
steps.summary: The merged result is validated strictly, but only problems the patch introduced or touched can reject it. Drift on anchors the user owns is flagged `userLocked` (the message says to tell the user or use `--actor user`); when it was already there and sits in an element the patch changed, it is downgraded to a warning, so it does not block the re-explanation.

steps.summary: A patch with any error is rejected as a whole and exits 1 without writing; otherwise, unless `--dry-run`, the file is written when something changed.
