tours.title: How xpl works: the full tour

steps.note: xpl is four packages plus the skill Claude follows: the CLI runs the commands, the indexer builds the symbol index, the viewer draws explainers, and core holds the schema and the pure logic. Core is imported by the other three; the three highlighted lines are one such import each.

The workflow starts with `xpl index`: the command calls buildIndex, which resolves references heuristically first and then lets a precise SCIP tool replace them for the files it described. Every reference records which of the two produced it, and the viewer draws the heuristic ones lighter.

`xpl apply` runs the patch through applyPatch as actor `llm` (or `user`); when a check fails nothing is written and the command exits 1. An llm patch also skips what the user authored (`skipUserOwned` warns `protected`) instead of overwriting it.

`xpl bundle` reads the viewer page and `injectBundle` writes the whole payload into it as a `<script id="xpl-data">` element; when the page opens, `loadBundle` reads that element back and core's `parseBundle` checks its schema. That is how an explainer becomes one self-contained HTML file.

A language pack turns one parsed file into plain facts and, by contract, assigns no ids or hashes; the framework does that. `assembleSymbols` gives each symbol the id `<file>#<path>`, numbers repeated paths `x`, `x~2`, and hashes its lines by the same rule anchors use later.

Precise references replace heuristic ones per file, not per language: a file the SCIP tool described takes its precise references, while the other files of that language keep their heuristic ones and are counted in `heuristicFiles`.

A patch is a shallow upsert by id: `convertFields` turns each field into stored form (`null` clears it, a field the user edited is skipped) and `mergeExisting` replaces the sent fields whole on a clone of the element, so an array like `members` or `steps` is replaced, not merged.

An anchor names code by `span` offsets from the symbol's first line or by `find` text, which `locateText` turns into the lines it touches. `makeAnchor` then hashes the trimmed non-blank lines of that range, so the pointer can be checked against the code later.

Any error left after the merge and the strict validation makes `fail()` return the caller's untouched explainer, so a rejected patch writes nothing. The command prints every issue at once, headed by `rejected: N errors, nothing was applied`, and exits 1.

A view draws the boxes its `include` names, not every symbol, so deriveGraph lifts each reference of a shown kind to the boxes that stand for its two ends: two different boxes give one derived arrow that counts the references, and an end with no box gives a stub. Calls between the shown files are derived this way, not stored.

A click ends in `codeFocus`: the element's resolved anchors become the highlighted lines, and when it has none its structure stands in (a symbol its own lines, a file the whole file, a directory its files).

The other direction: for each line under the caret, `lookup` returns the elements with the smallest range that contains it, so a step's call site beats the lifeline or file around it. Every concept is a candidate too, so the same caret can light up a concept card.

Spans are stored as offsets from the symbol's first line, so code added above the symbol just moves the base and the anchor is `moved` with no search. When lines are added or removed inside the symbol, the hash no longer matches at the expected lines, so `searchSpan` looks for it in the symbol and the anchor gets a new span.

If the text itself changed and is nowhere in the symbol, the anchor is `drifted` and keeps its old hash. `reresolveExplainer` files the drifted anchors of llm elements as elements to re-explain, and those of any other owner as left alone.

A re-explain is safe because the llm actor reads provenance first: an existing item with origin `user` is skipped whole, and a field listed in `userFields` keeps the user's value while the other fields of that element are merged.

Two design choices tie it together: what static analysis finds is derived, not stored (a stored edge with a derived edge's id adds its label, summary and anchors to that edge), and the skill explains what a view shows and leaves the rest for `expand`. Under `xpl view`, the viewer's Explain button queues a request for it.

tours.title: How xpl works in five minutes

steps.note: xpl makes explainers: diagrams linked both ways to the code they explain. It is four packages plus the skill Claude follows, and core, the schema and the pure logic, is imported by the other three.

Claude writes patches, never UI, and `xpl apply` builds each anchor from the index: `makeAnchor` finds the code and stores a hash of its lines. Later `resolveWith` compares that hash with the code as it is, so an anchor whose code changed becomes `drifted` (or `moved` if the same text sits elsewhere in the symbol) instead of silently pointing at different code.

`xpl bundle` reads the viewer page and `injectBundle` writes the whole payload into it as a `<script id="xpl-data">` element; when the page opens, `loadBundle` reads that element back and core's `parseBundle` checks its schema. That is how an explainer becomes one self-contained HTML file.

A click ends in `codeFocus`: the element's resolved anchors become the highlighted lines, and when it has none its structure stands in (a symbol its own lines, a file the whole file, a directory its files).

The other direction: for each line under the caret, `lookup` returns the elements with the smallest range that contains it, so a step's call site beats the lifeline or file around it. Every concept is a candidate too, so the same caret can light up a concept card.

When the code changes, `xpl resolve` re-finds every anchor: `missing` when its symbol is gone, `moved` when its text is still in the symbol, `drifted` when the text itself changed. The drifted llm elements are what it lists to re-explain.
